title: The Willow Creek Twins

subtitle.text: It was Saturday, and Katie Donovan sat on the kitchen floor petting Magoo, the family dog.
Her twin sister, Joy, was at the big round table, waiting for a snack.
Grandpa, the best cook in the family, had just baked brownies.
"Mmm," said Katie. "I love brownies!"
Just then Mom looked toward the County Road and said,
"The mail truck is coming, girls.
It’s turning the corner."
Katie jumped up. "Let’s go, Magoo!"
She and the hound raced through the house and out the front door.
Magoo followed Katie all the way down the driveway.
Katie hardly ever got any mail, except birthday cards.
And those were sent to Katie and Joy Donovan.
But both girls still liked to collect the mail when it came.
The mail truck rumbled to a stop at 10 Blackberry Road.
The mailman leaned out of the window.
"Hello, Magoo!" he called and gave the mail to Katie.
"Hello, Jeff," said Katie.
Jeff looked at her closely.
"Which twin are you?" he asked.
Katie sighed. "I’m KATIE."
"I always get you two mixed-up," said Jeff.
Then he drove off down the road.
"We’re totally different . . . ,"
mumbled Katie as the mail truck disappeared in a cloud of dust.
Katie liked having a sister who was her identical twin.
But she hated it when people mixed them up, which happened all the time.
"You know which one I am, don’t you, Magoo?" whispered Katie.
Magoo sniffed her hand. "That’s right.
Joy and I smell different, don’t we?"
The house smelled like brownies.
"Mail delivery!" Katie called out.
She read the name on the first envelope.
"For John Donovan—from Sunshine Seed Company.""Great!"
said Grandpa. "My corn seeds!" Grandpa
would be planting the garden soon. "Here’s
a letter for Debra Donovan," said Katie, flipping through the mail. Mom
was looking at a book about Missouri birds. "Thanks,
honey," she said. "And for
Steve A. Donovan—the new Green Zine! " exclaimed Katie. This
was a magazine all about recycling. Dad
owned the Willow Creek Recycling Center. "The
rest is junk mail," said Katie. "Nothing
for us today, Joy. Unless
you want a chicken catalog! It’s
from a place called the Cackle Farm." She said with a grin. "Okay,"
said Joy as Katie grabbed a brownie from the table. "Okay?"
echoed Katie in surprise. "Okay,
I’ll look at the catalog," repeated Joy. "Really?"
Katie handed it to her. "You’re interested in chickens?" "Yep."
Joy flipped through the catalog. "Hey,
I didn’t know chickens came in all these colors," she said. "Look
at this one, Katie!" "I
don’t like chickens," Katie said. " You like them."
"You’re no fun sometimes," Joy complained.
Katie ignored her sister.
Instead she followed Dad, who was carrying a bucket out to the compost bin.
"Dad," she asked slowly, "how can you tell I’m Katie and not Joy?"
"Oh, that’s easy.
I just . . . Well . . ." Then Dad grinned.
"I know. Your freckles!
You have fourteen freckles on your nose.
Joy has twelve!"
"Oh, Dad!" Katie moaned.
"You don’t believe me? Go count them!"
Katie rolled her eyes and walked back inside.
Her father was teasing her.
He didn’t understand that sometimes it was hard to be a twin.
Joy was still looking at the catalog.
"We can buy these chickens when they are tiny chicks and raise them."
"Then what would we do?
Make fried chicken? HA!" joked Katie.
"We wouldn’t eat them!" Joy said. "We’d eat their eggs!"
"What’s wrong with the eggs from Tucker’s Grocery?" asked Katie.
Joy made a face.
"Chickens are fun, Katie—not like you right now!"
Katie looked away.
She knew she was being a little mean to her sister.
But for some reason, she couldn’t help it today.
It was Sunday morning, and Grandpa was making everyone pancakes.
Joy was still in her pajamas and still talking about chickens.
"This one has a blue tail," said Joy.
"And this one has feathers on its feet!"
Mom smiled. "They look like house slippers."
Grandpa gave Joy a plate of pancakes and looked over her shoulder at the catalog.
"See that one with the black and white stripes?" he said.
"We had a hen like that when I was a boy.
Sometimes she slept in my lap—just like a cat."
Dad smiled. "So Joy," he said, "do you think we should get some chickens?"
Joy’s eyes opened wide, and a big smile spread across her face.
"Oh, Dad! Could we?
Could we buy some little chicks?"
"They won’t be little for long," warned Mom.
"They’ll become big chickens.
Would you take care of them?
Would you feed them and give them water?"
"Yes, I promise," said Joy.
"And I’d gather the eggs too."
"I could make some delicious omelets with those fresh eggs," said Grandpa.
"Where’s Katie?" asked Joy, jumping up from the table.
She ran to the stairway and called, "Come downstairs, Katie!"
Upstairs Katie didn’t hear her sister.
She was busy staring at herself in the bathroom mirror.
Jellybean, the cat, was sitting in the doorway, licking her gray fur.
"Here we go," Katie whispered as she picked up the scissors.
Jellybean stopped licking and watched Katie with round, yellow eyes.
Downstairs Dad was talking.
"It’s good for the planet when we raise our own food," he said.
"I hope I can remember how to take care of baby chickens," said Grandpa.
"You have to teach me, Grandpa,"
replied Joy as she sat back down at the table.
She’d given up trying to get Katie’s attention.
"I’ll bring home a book on the subject tomorrow," said Mom.
She worked part-time at the Willow Creek library.
Suddenly everyone looked up at the ceiling.
They heard Katie’s footsteps in the hallway above.
Then they heard her pounding down the stairs.
"Here she comes," said Joy.
"Good morning, world!" Katie exclaimed as she popped into the kitchen.
She twirled on her bare feet.
"Notice anything different about me?"
Magoo, who had been napping in the corner, opened his eyes.
"Yes, I noticed that you ran down the steps with scissors!" scolded Mom.
"That’s really dangerous."
Katie looked down at the scissors in her hand.
"Oops," she said. "Sorry."
"You’ve done something to your hair," stated Dad.
"You’ve got bangs!" Joy burst out.
"Ta-da!" exclaimed Katie.
Joy frowned. "But Katie," she said, "now we look different."
"That’s right," Katie said happily.
"From now on, I’m the one with bangs."
She sat down at the table.
"Grandpa, may I have some pancakes, please?"
"You did a good job, Katie," Mom commented.
Joy looked around the table, upset.
"But . . . do we still look like twins?"
"Sure you do," said Dad.
"Nope," corrected Katie. "We look completely different."
Then Mom spoke up. "Joy, tell Katie about the chickens."
"Chickens?" repeated Katie.
"Yes," said Joy. "We’re getting chicks from the Cackle Farm!"
Katie stared at her sister.
"What will we have to do?"
"Lots!" Joy was smiling again.
"You see, they have to live indoors for a while.
We have to keep them warm and watch them every minute."
When Katie thought of the cute little chicks, she almost smiled.
But then she remembered that she was the Donovan twin who didn’t like chickens.
Joy noticed Katie’s blank expression.
"Aren’t you excited?" she asked.
Katie shrugged and poured syrup on her pancakes.
"Last chance for pancakes, folks," Grandpa announced.
"Joy and I have to get this kitchen cleaned up.
We’ve got chicken plans!"
The next day Katie and Joy rode their bicycles to Boone Elementary School.
They were both excited.
Katie couldn’t wait for everyone to see her new bangs.
And Joy wanted to tell everyone about the chickens.
"There’s Luke!" shouted Joy.
She waved at a boy in a T-shirt that said "I DIG WORMS."
Luke was Katie and Joy’s cousin.
"Joy," said Katie, "why don’t you wait until Mr. Higgins starts the science lesson?
Then tell everybody about the chicks.
Learning about animals is part of science."
Joy hesitated. "Well, if you think so," she said.
"I guess I could wait until science."
But Katie didn’t wait to share her news.
"Hey, Luke! I’ve got bangs!
Now nobody will mix me up with Joy!"
"Oh. That’s good, I guess," Luke replied.
"How’s your bait business?" asked Katie.
Luke collected earthworms and sold them to fishermen at the gas station.
"Excellent," said Luke.
"On Saturday I sold eight cups of worms for a dollar each.
Wait until summer.
I won’t be able to keep up with the demand."
"Here comes Laura!" exclaimed Joy.
Laura Layman was in the third grade too.
"What’s new?" Laura asked.
"I’ve got bangs," Katie blurted out.
"And I’ve got something exciting to tell everyone," Joy whispered to Laura.
"But I can’t say it yet."
Ms. Olson, the school principal, stood outside the front door.
"Good morning, twins," she said. "Good morning, Luke, Laura."
"Good morning, Ms. Olson," said Katie.
"From now on remember—Katie is the one with bangs."
"Okay. That’s nice to know," replied Ms. Olson.
Mr. Higgins waited by the door to the third-grade classroom.
"Hello, Luke. Hello, Laura," he said. "Hello, twins."
"Katie here," stated Katie. "I’m the one with bangs."
She thought, "It’s going to be a great day." The
first activity of the day was a math worksheet. Katie
got three division problems wrong. Joy
solved them all. During
spelling time Katie spelled "cheese" with a z instead of an s .
Joy spelled every word right.
When it was time for art, Katie’s clay horse would not stand up.
But Joy’s clay sheep looked perfect.
"What is happening to my great day?" wondered Katie.
She had a feeling that things would get worse.
Science was next, and that meant Joy would soon have everyone’s attention.
First, Luke showed the class a creepy earthworm he dug up.
It was 23 centimeters long!
Next, Joy raised her hand.
Katie jumped out of her seat. "Guess what?"
Mr. Higgins and the class looked at Katie.
"We’re getting baby chickens," said Katie.
She heard Joy gasp.
"That’s big news," said Mr. Higgins. "How old will they be?"
"Um, they’ll be really little," Katie said quickly.
"One day old," Joy answered.
Mr. Higgins turned to Joy. "Oh," he said.
Then he looked back at Katie.
"How many chicks are you getting?"
"Maybe three," replied Katie.
She looked over at Joy, who narrowed her eyes at Katie.
"Six," Joy corrected her.
"What do chicks eat?" asked Mr. Higgins.
"Are you getting a rooster?" asked Luke.
"Will they miss their mother?" asked Laura.
Katie was sorry that she had opened her big mouth.
She had ruined things for Joy.
And now she couldn’t answer a single question.
She looked over at Joy.
"Well," Joy said, taking over, "first, they will have special feed."
She pulled out her chicken catalog, and everyone gathered around Joy’s desk.
"Here are the kinds of chickens we picked out," she explained proudly.
Katie stayed at her desk, listening in silence.
Katie knew she had made a big mistake at school.
She should have let Joy tell the big news about the chickens.
"I need some exciting news of my own,"
thought Katie as she finished setting the table.
"Something bigger than bangs."
"Suppertime!" called Grandpa. "My famous spaghetti and meatballs."
The family sat down at the kitchen table, and Mom started filling plates.
Joy shot a look at Katie.
"Everyone asked me a million questions about the baby chickens today.
And Mr. Higgins asked me to bring some chicks to school in a few weeks!"
Katie felt her face turn red.
"Luke brought an earthworm to school," she said quickly.
"It was 23 centimeters long."
"Oh my!" exclaimed Mom.
"I don’t like worms," said Joy. "They’re yucky."
"I think worms are cool," explained Katie.
"Maybe we should all sell worms too!" suggested Dad, laughing.
"Not me," said Joy with a shiver.
"I brought home a sturdy cardboard box from the recycling center today," said Dad.
"It will make a good house for the chicks."
"I bought chicken feed and some other stuff at the store today," said Grandpa.
"Everything is in the spare room."
Katie suddenly jumped up from her chair. "Aha!" she exclaimed.
"I got it!" Everyone stared at her.
"What?" asked Mom.
"I’m going to help Luke sell worms!"
Katie dashed out of the kitchen and up the stairs to her room.
"That child is full of surprises," said Mom, shaking her head.
Joy didn’t say anything.
She was still a little mad at Katie for blurting out the news about the chicks.
"Well, what are we waiting for?" asked Dad.
"The chicks should arrive in the mail tomorrow.
Let’s get to work!"
They all headed upstairs to the spare room.
The supplies Grandpa had bought were piled on the floor.
Dad cleared off a table and set his big cardboard box on top.
"A chick house is called a brooder," explained Mom.
She was sitting on the bed, reading from her library book How to Raise Chickens.
"We need to put holes in the sides so air can flow through the box."
"I can do that," replied Dad.
Joy picked up some shopping bags and opened them on the bed.
"Look at this stuff!" she cried happily.
"Here’s the chicken feeder! And a water jar!"
"Here’s the heat lamp," said Grandpa.
"The lamp should be about half a meter above the chicks," explained Mom.
"The babies need to be kept warm."
Grandpa clamped the lamp on the box.
Joy emptied a bag of wood shavings into the box.
As she spread them out, Grandpa filled the feeder and the water jar.
He put them in the box, and Mom added a thermometer.
"Ready?" asked Mom.
"Ready!" cried Joy.
Suddenly something flew through the air and landed right in the brooder!
"Oh, Jellybean!" cried Joy.
She put her arms around Jellybean’s belly and lifted her out of the box.
Jellybean screeched.
"Go away!" scolded Joy. "No cats allowed!"
Jellybean ran down the hallway to the twins’ bedroom.
Katie was talking on the telephone.
"Okay, Luke," she said. "Tomorrow night.
A flashlight . . . a bucket . . . a rag.
I’ll have everything ready.
Thanks, partner!" She hung up the phone.
"Big news, Jellybean!" said Katie happily.
"I’m in the bait business!"
"Here comes Jeff!" cried Joy.
The mail truck came up the driveway.
Joy and Magoo leaped off the front porch.
"Special delivery!" Jeff called and held a cardboard box out of the window.
"Are they in there?"
asked Joy, jumping up and down with excitement.
"Steady now," said Jeff.
He laid the box carefully in Joy's hands.
"I hear them," she whispered. "They're moving around inside."
She turned and started back toward the house.
Magoo sniffed at the bottom of the box as Jeff drove off.
Grandpa, Mom, and even Katie, waited at the front door.
"Follow me, everybody," called Joy.
She and the chicks went upstairs to the spare room.
"I turned on the heat lamp," said Mom.
She checked the thermometer in the box.
"Perfect! Nice and warm."
The chicks were chirping in their box.
"Do you hear them?" asked Joy.
"Yes, Joy. They want to come out and meet you," replied Grandpa.
"Here are the scissors."
Joy cut the bands around the box and lifted the lid.
"Ooh!" squealed Joy when she saw the little balls of fluff inside.
"Aren't they sweet?" said Mom. "Look, Katie."
Katie had been standing back in the doorway.
But now she stepped forward and peeked in the box.
"One, two, three, four, five, six," counted Katie. "All there."
"Let's put them in the box before they get cold," suggested Grandpa.
One by one, Joy placed the chicks in the box.
Mom had her chicken book open.
"Now, it's important that they eat and drink," she stated.
"Have they found the water, Joy?"
Joy picked up a chick and put it next to the water feeder.
"Look!" she exclaimed and clapped her hands. "It's drinking!"
Just then Dad stepped into the spare room.
As usual his work clothes were dirty.
Katie gave him a big hug anyway.
"Everyone's looking at the chicks, Dad," she said.
"But I have work to do in my room."
"Well, look at these babies!"
exclaimed Dad with a grin as he looked into the box.
The chicks had been drinking water and pecking at their food.
But now they were getting quiet.
One little chick tipped over on its side and lay completely still.
"What's wrong?" asked Joy, worried.
She poked the chick lightly with her finger.
Its eyes popped open.
"The little one just fell asleep," whispered Grandpa. "She's tired."
They watched the chicks fall asleep, one by one.
Joy put her finger to her lips. "Shh," she said.
Everyone tiptoed out of the spare room.
Joy pointed to a sign she had made for the door: "NO CATS ALLOWED!"
Down the hall Katie was hard at work.
She was taping a piece of red plastic over a flashlight.
Luke had told her how to do it.
Jellybean was sprawled on Katie's bed watching every move Katie made.
"Jellybean," said Katie, "did you know that earthworms in Australia can grow to be three and a half meters long?"
Jellybean blinked while Katie tore off another piece of tape.
"And did you know that some earthworms live to be eight years old?"
Jellybean blinked again.
"HA! That's how old I am," exclaimed Katie as she smoothed the tape into place. "There!"
She closed the curtains and turned off the light switch.
Then Katie turned on the flashlight.
A spooky red beam flashed around the room.
"Great!" she said. "I'm ready for worm hunting!"
The sun had set, and tiny bugs darted around the back-porch light.
Mom put a baseball cap on Katie's head and said,
"The air is getting cool."
Luke tied a big rag onto Katie's belt loop.
"What's that for?" Katie asked.
"You'll see," said Luke. "Do you have your bucket?"
"Yep," said Katie.
"Flashlight?"
"Yep," replied Katie. "I'm ready to hunt worms."
"Don't go too far from the house," said Mom.
"And don't be gone long!"
Katie and Luke stepped off the porch and headed into the darkness.
"The grass is all wet," said Katie.
"That's good," explained Luke. "Earthworms like it cool and wet."
"My toes don't," replied Katie.
Her sneakers felt soggy.
"Walk softly," warned Luke.
"If they feel our footsteps, they will slip right back into the ground."
"I thought we had to dig for worms," said Katie.
"That's the hard way," replied Luke.
"This is the easy way."
They stepped carefully through the grass.
There was no sound except the croaking of the toads down by the creek.
"Okay, stop here," instructed Luke. "Turn on your flashlight."
Katie flashed the red beam back and forth over the grass.
"See," he whispered. "The worms are out!"
Luke was right!
Everywhere the light shone, Katie could see worms gleaming in the grass.
"Ooh, creepy," she whispered.
Luke gave her a look.
"Sorry," said Katie. "I mean, ooh, cool!"
"Now watch me," ordered Luke.
He bent over one of the shining worms and grabbed it.
Then he slowly pulled the worm out of its hole.
"Got it," said Luke. "It's a big one."
He plopped it into his bucket. "Now you try."
Katie stooped down beside Luke and quickly spotted an earthworm.
She reached out and grabbed.
"Got it!" she said.
She held her hand up to show Luke.
But her hand was empty.
"It got away!" she cried.
"And my hand is all slimy!"
"That's what your rag is for," explained Luke.
"Dry your hand and try again.
This time, grab it closer to the middle."
As Katie wiped her hand on her rag, she spotted another worm.
She slowly stretched out her hand and grabbed it around its middle. She pulled.
"It won't come out. It's holding on," she said.
"Keep pulling," instructed Luke.
"The worm will get tired and let go."
Katie pulled some more until the earthworm came sliding out.
"Hooray!" she exclaimed. "I got one!"
"Okay," said Luke. "Toss it in the bucket."
A little later, Katie and Luke ran through the back door, into the kitchen.
Everyone was sitting around the table, and Grandpa was serving slices of apple pie.
"I've got worms!" shouted Katie.
"Not in the house," said Mom.
"Oh, right," said Katie.
She opened the back door and set her bucket on the porch.
"Now, before you have your pie," said Mom, "why don't you show Luke our new chicks?"
Katie sighed. She wanted to talk about her worms.
"Come on, Luke," she said softly.
Katie led her cousin out of the kitchen and up the stairs.
She opened the door to the spare room and pulled him over to the chick box.
"There they are," she said.
"They're cute, but a lot of trouble.
You have to feed them and clean up their stinky poop."
"Worms are more fun," stated Luke.
"That's for sure," agreed Katie.
"Now, let's go eat some pie."
The two worm hunters didn't notice another hunter in the hallway.
Jellybean had been waiting silently in the dark.
She crept toward the spare room.
The door had been left open just a crack.
Jellybean put one paw on the door and pushed.
The chicks chirped inside their box as the door swung open.
"Just in time, kids!" Grandpa said to Luke and Katie.
"There are two slices of apple pie left."
"My favorite!" exclaimed Luke.
He and Katie joined the family around the kitchen table.
"So you caught some worms," said Dad.
"You should have seen me," bragged Katie.
She grabbed an imaginary worm from the air.
"Got it!" she shouted.
"Stop right there!" said Mom.
She was looking at Katie's hand—her very dirty hand.
"Yuck," said Joy.
"Uh-oh," said Katie.
She looked at Luke.
Luke looked at his own hands.
"Gross," he said.
"Come on," grumbled Katie, standing up.
"Let's go wash up and put these dirty rags in the hamper."
Katie and Luke climbed back up the stairs.
"Don't eat our pie!" Katie called down the steps.
"Mealtime is no time for worm slime," Luke said with a chuckle.
"Hey, you just made a rhyme about slime," said Katie, giggling.
"So did you!" exclaimed Luke.
Katie led the way down the hall, past the spare room.
"Listen to those chicks," said Luke. "They are loud!"
"They sure are!" complained Katie. Then she stopped, worried.
"Wait a minute. Is that door open?"
She looked back toward the spare room.
"It should be closed!"
Katie and Luke hurried into the spare room.
Katie switched on the light.
"JELLYBEAN!" she cried.
The cat's head was in the box.
Everything happened so fast.
Jellybean leaped up and landed on the desk.
Luke tried to grab Jellybean, but the cat leaped to the floor.
Then Jellybean ran out the door and down the hall.
A white ball of fluff was in her mouth.
"COME BACK HERE!" screamed Katie. "Mom! Dad! Help!"
Katie and Luke chased Jellybean into Mom and Dad's bedroom.
"Where is she?" cried Katie.
She dropped to the floor and looked under the bed.
Katie could see Jellybean's yellow eyes shining in the dark.
A white chick was in the cat's mouth.
The frightened chick cheeped loudly.
Katie pulled her head out from under the bed.
The whole family was looking down at her with wide eyes.
"Jellybean has a chick," she said grimly.
Joy gasped.
"Uh-oh," said Dad.
"Not good," added Grandpa.
"Don't worry," said Katie.
"I think I can get it back."
Then she wiggled under the bed, trying not to panic.
"Hello, Jellybean," she said softly, facing the cat.
"What have you got?"
Looking like a proud hunter, Jellybean held on to the chick.
"Come on, Jellybean," Katie whispered.
"Let me have the baby chick."
Katie slowly reached out.
She gently cupped her hands underneath the chick.
Jellybean opened her mouth, and the chick fell into Katie's hands.
"Thank you, Jellybean," whispered Katie.
Then she wiggled out from under the bed.
"Got it!" Katie said as she stood up.
"Thank you, Katie!" exclaimed Joy.
"Let's check on the others," said Mom.
Everyone rushed to the box.
"One, two, three, four, five," counted Katie.
She put the white chick back with the others.
"Six," she said.
Luke was standing in the doorway.
He looked unhappy.
"This was my fault," he said.
"I left the door open."
"No," replied Katie. "It was my fault."
She looked at Joy.
"I forgot to make sure the door was closed. I'm sorry, Joy."
Joy gave Katie a hug.
"We still have six chicks," she said.
"So everything is okay."
Katie nodded. "That was close," she murmured.
"Well," Grandpa spoke up, "I still have two slices of pie downstairs.
Anybody interested?"
"Absolutely!" said Katie.
"Let's go!" exclaimed Luke.
"Wait a minute!" warned Mom. "Forgetting something?"
Katie and Luke looked at each other.
They both held up their hands.
"Worm slime!" they cried.
The third graders had just put away their math books.
Suddenly they heard a buzz from the speaker on the wall.
The voice of the principal, Ms. Olson, rang through the classroom.
"Joy Donovan, please come to the office."
"Grandpa is here with the chicks!" cried Joy.
"Hooray!" cheered Katie.
"May I go to the office, Mr. Higgins?"
asked Joy as she jumped up from her desk.
"Yes, you may," said the teacher.
Joy stopped at Katie's desk.
"Go ahead and draw the chicken," she whispered loudly.
Mr. Higgins nodded to Katie, and she walked to the whiteboard.
She took a marker and drew a big chicken.
Just as Katie finished the tail, Joy marched back into the room.
Grandpa walked behind her with a large cardboard box.
"Let's all say hello to Mr. Donovan," instructed Mr. Higgins.
The third graders clapped and called, "Hello, Mr. Donovan!"
"Hello, kids," Grandpa said, smiling.
He carried the box to a table in the front of the room.
Then he sat down on a small chair.
"I've already seen the chicks,"
Luke whispered to the boy next to him.
"They're cheeping!" cried Laura Layman.
Joy walked to the front of the class and stood beside Katie.
"We're going to look at the chicks in the box.
But first Katie will tell you about her drawing."
"In five or six months, these little chicks will look like this.
This is a grown-up hen.
That's what you call a female chicken," Katie explained to the class.
"Here is the hen's beak." She pointed to the whiteboard.
"This wavy thing on top is called a comb."
She tapped her finger on the comb.
"And this floppy part under the beak is called a wattle."
"Cool," said Luke. "Where are the feet?"
The whole class laughed.
Katie had run out of space on the board and hadn't drawn the feet.
"You're silly, Luke," replied Katie.
"Thank you, Katie," said Mr. Higgins. "That was very helpful."
Now it was Joy's turn.
"Our chicks aren't grown up yet," she said.
"They're about two weeks old."
She lifted the lid off the box.
All the third graders jumped out of their seats and gathered around the box.
"Hey!" exclaimed Luke. "Their hair looks funny.
It's sticking out."
The chicks were cheeping and hopping around inside the box.
Joy lifted a chick from the box.
"They're getting real feathers on their tails and wings."
"This one has little horns," exclaimed one of her classmates.
"That is where its comb is starting to grow," explained Joy.
"Why do some have white legs and some have yellow legs?" asked Luke.
"They're just different," said Joy.
"Are the two white ones twins?" asked Laura.
"They look alike."
"They look alike, but they're not the same," said Katie.
She picked up one of the white chicks and put it in Laura's hand.
"This one is nice and calm, but the other one―"
The other white chick chirped and ran around in circles.
Everyone looked closely into the box as the chick tripped over the feeder.
It knocked into some of the other chicks.
"What's it doing?" asked Luke.
Suddenly the squawking chick jumped and flapped its little wings.
"It's trying to fly!" cried Laura.
All the children laughed.
"See?" said Joy. "The chicks look alike.
But they're really different."
"Just like us!" Katie couldn't help saying.
"Hooray for Katie and Joy's chicks!" Laura said.
All the third graders clapped and cheered.
Katie and Joy looked at each other and smiled.
Then they cheered too!
The third graders were restless.
They wanted to be playing outdoors, not sitting in the classroom.
Mr. Higgins stood in front of the class.
"What happens in spring?" he asked.
"We plan for summer vacation!" said Katie.
"True," said Mr. Higgins.
"But it's not time for that yet, Katie.
Who has another answer?"
"Flowers bloom!" said Laura.
"Birds build nests!" said Joy.
"Good," said Mr. Higgins. "What about the weather?"

of walnuts dropped—again! I thought I would never
reach my goal." "What did you
do?" asked AJ. "Well, I just kept picking
walnuts," said Joy. "But Katie and Olivia called Luke, Larry,
Laura, and Carlos. They all showed up on Sunday morning
to help me." "Me
too," said Manny. "Yes! You
too," said Joy. "With so many people, we were able to fill the cart
quickly," said Olivia. "Whenever the cart was full, Mr. Donovan and Joy took it to the nut-buying
station," said Laura. "We filled the cart
three times." "I did better than my goal,"
said Joy. "I earned one hundred eleven dollars and fifty-five cents!—thanks to
my friends." "Is your fiddle fixed?"
asked AJ. "It’s in the shop,"
said Joy. "Soon it will be as good
as new!" "Just like my ankle!"
said Katie. The hay wagon bounced down the trail. Mr. Ferguson started
a song. Old Dan Tucker was a
mighty man. He washed his face in a
frying pan. The kids
joined in. Joy played an
imaginary fiddle. He combed his hair with a
wagon wheel. And died with a toothache in his
heel. The kids sang, and Mr. Ferguson drove into the
woods. They hadn’t gone too far when Carlos saw
something. "It looks like a bonfire!" he
said. "It is a bonfire," said
Laura. "It’s AJ’s dad," cried
Katie. "You’re finally here," shouted Mr. Morgan, AJ and Emily’s
dad. "I thought I might have to roast the hot dogs all by
myself." Everyone jumped out of the hay
wagon. "Welcome to AJ’s birthday bonfire!" said
Emily. "Who wants hot apple
cider?" "AJ has to make a birthday wish!" said
Katie. "I can’t tell you my birthday wish," said
AJ. "Then it won’t come true!"
Joy smiled at the little boy.
"Well, make another wish then.
It doesn’t have to be your birthday wish," she said.
"And then you can tell us!" added Katie.
"Okay," said AJ.
"I wish to have the biggest birthday hayride in Willow Creek next year!
I’ll invite everyone!"

episodes.title: A New Year, a New Project

subtitle.text: It was the Monday after New Year's Day.
Joy was sitting in science class listening to Ms. Barrow talk about the weather.
She passed a note to Katie that said: No more rain!
Katie nodded and sighed.
It had been raining in Willow Creek for days.
Joy wished it would snow!
"Science books away, please," Ms. Barrow said.
It was time for social studies.
"Who knows what holiday is in January?"
Laura raised her hand.
"Martin Luther King Jr. Day," she said.
"Right! What did Martin Luther King Jr. do?" Ms. Barrow asked.
"He wanted black people and white people to be equal," Carlos answered.
"So they could go to the same schools and live in the same neighborhoods."
"Yes. So he gave speeches and led marches for freedom," said Ms. Barrow.
"He fought for something he believed in.
That made him one of America's great leaders."
Ms. Barrow wrote "LEADERS" on the board.
"Our next social studies project is going to be about American leaders."
She passed out a worksheet that said:
"What Makes a Leader?"
"You'll all choose someone famous in history and give a report on him or her.
Explain what made this person a great leader.
Then I want you to try to live like your leader for one week."
"That sounds interesting," thought Joy.
"I might choose George Washington.
Does that mean I have to wear a funny hat with three corners?" Katie asked.
Ms. Barrow smiled. "No, Katie.
But now and then, you can ask yourself, 'What would George Washington do if he were me?'"
"I want to do my project on George Washington," Carlos said.
"I thought of him first."
Katie rolled her eyes.
"But okay. I choose Abraham Lincoln instead."
"I'm going to do Martin Luther King!" Luke announced.
All the fourth graders began shouting out names of famous leaders.
Joy sat quietly at her desk, thinking.
She wanted to pick the perfect leader for her project.
When the twins got home from school, they found Grandpa in the kitchen.
He was lifting a tray of chocolate chip cookies out of the oven.
"Just in time, girls," he said.
"Yum! Thanks, Grandpa," Katie said, plopping herself down at the table.
Joy went to the refrigerator.
She poured a glass of milk for herself and for Katie.
"Grandpa, who is your favorite American leader?" Joy asked.
"Hmm. Probably President Franklin D. Roosevelt.
He helped our country out of the Great Depression.
Many people had lost everything—their jobs, their houses, even all their money.
And Roosevelt found ways to help many of these people," Grandpa answered. "Why?"
"We're doing a project on leaders at school," Katie said, her mouth full of cookie.
"I chose Abraham Lincoln.
He was brave enough to say he didn't like slavery, even when it made him unpopular."
"And he worked very hard during America's Civil War," Grandpa added.
"Lincoln is a great choice for your project."
Joy frowned. She still didn't know which leader to choose.
"Oh! It's already four thirty!" she cried, glancing up at the clock.
"I have to take care of the chickens, do my homework, and practice my fiddle!"
"And wash the dishes later," Grandpa reminded her.
"Because Dad and I are leaving for South Dakota right after dinner."
Joy had forgotten that Grandpa and Dad were leaving tonight for their annual fishing trip.
That meant she and Katie would have more chores this week.
She jumped up from her chair.
It was going to be a busy week!
The next morning Katie and Joy sat at the kitchen table.
Katie frowned at the bowl in front of her.
"We're having cereal?" she asked her mother.
Grandpa usually made them oatmeal or pancakes.
"Sorry, girls," Mom said.
"Grandpa's away, and I have to get ready to go to work."
Joy had an idea.
"I'll get some eggs to make us an omelet!"
She put on her raincoat and ran out to the chicken coop.
"Good morning, girls," she called to the chickens.
Four of them clucked around her ankles as she opened the gate.
She reached her hand into the nest box.
No eggs! That was strange.
"The chickens are being lazy," Joy announced back in the kitchen.
"No eggs today!"
Mom looked up from the sink, where she was washing dishes.
"That's unusual. But you girls have to leave for school soon anyway.
Hurry up and eat your cereal.
And don't forget to come to the library after school."
In class Ms. Barrow announced that they'd be working on their social studies projects today.
"For the next thirty minutes, please work by yourself," Ms. Barrow said.
"To find information about your leader, you may use the Internet or books."
Joy looked around.
Larry had pulled out a book about President Franklin D. Roosevelt.
Laura was reading a book on Abraham Lincoln.
It seemed like most kids had already gone to the public library.
They were ready to start their projects, but Joy hadn't even chosen her leader yet!
Ms. Barrow saw her looking around.
"Here, Joy. Try this."
Ms. Barrow handed her a book called Great American Biographies
. "You might find someone you like in
here." "Thanks," Joy
said. She opened the book and tried to
read. But she couldn't
concentrate. She thought about the list of chores Mom had put on the refrigerator this morning.
She thought about what she had brought for lunch.
Then she started wondering what Dad and Grandpa were doing on their fishing trip.
Katie jumped up from a computer and ran to Joy's desk.
"Did you know that Abraham Lincoln used to walk miles just to borrow a book?" Katie whispered.
Joy shook her head.
"He loved to read and write," Katie added.
Joy shrugged. "So I think we should walk to the library after school today!
Get it? Like Abe Lincoln!"
Joy looked at her sister and sighed.
"Katie, we were going to walk there anyway."
"You're right," Katie said.
"But I'm still going to use it in my report. HA!"
She rushed back to the computer.
After school it was still raining.
"This really makes me feel like a leader!" Katie said.
She stomped on a frozen puddle, cracking the ice.
"We're walking through the freezing rain to get books because we believe in . . . education!"
Joy rolled her eyes and continued walking quietly.
At the library Mrs. Donovan helped Joy find lots of books on leaders.
"Mom," Joy said slowly.
"Who should I do my leader project on?"
"I can help you pick books, honey.
But I can't pick your leader for you.
That's something only you can decide."
Mom patted the stack of books and smiled.
"You'll find someone good soon. Don't worry."
After dinner Joy practiced her fiddle until bedtime.
Then she grabbed a flashlight.
"I'm going to check for eggs!" she called.
She headed outside toward the chicken coop.
"One, two, three, four, five, six." Joy counted the chickens.
"All there!" Then she shined her light into the nest box.
It was empty again!
Joy flashed her light around the coop.
She saw something in the mud.
Were those chicken footprints or something else?
"Mom! Katie!" cried Joy, running into the kitchen.
"Someone—or something—is stealing our eggs!"
"What? Someone is stealing our eggs?" cried Katie.
"I think so," said Joy.
"There are still no eggs in the henhouse.
It doesn't make sense. And . . ." Joy lowered her voice.
"I found footprints."
Mom gasped. Katie's eyes grew wide.
"Whose footprints?" asked Katie.
"I don't know. But they're small," said Joy.
"Like a cat's? Or a raccoon's?" asked Katie.
"We need to investigate," said Mom.
"The chickens could be in danger!" said Katie.
"I'll call Grandpa.
He'll know what to do!" said Joy.
"Yes, but it's pretty late," Mom said.
"You can call tomorrow."
But Joy was already dialing.
"Please, Mom? This is important."
A few seconds later, Joy frowned as she hung up the phone.
"It went straight to Grandpa's voicemail so I didn't leave a message."
"See what happens tomorrow, honey," Mom said.
"You have more important things to worry about right now.
Like your homework."
Joy sighed. She wasn't happy, but she'd have to wait.
The next morning Olivia met the twins by the front door of Boone Elementary.
"I watched the best movie on Martin Luther King last night," she said.
"It really helped me with my project."
"These projects are fun, aren't they?" said Laura.
"Are you living like Martin Luther King?"
"I sure am!" said Olivia.
"Yesterday I tried a peaceful protest when my mom told me it was time for bed."
"Cool!" said Katie. "What did you do?"
"I sat quietly in front of the TV and refused to move," said Olivia.
"Did it work?" Laura asked.
"I got to watch 15 more minutes of TV.
So I guess it did!" The girls laughed.
"Good morning, fourth graders."
Ms. Olson greeted them as they walked into their classroom.
"Ms. Barrow is sick today, so Mr. Curtis will be your teacher.
Class, please say hello to Mr. Curtis."
"Good morning, Mr. Curtis," the fourth graders said.
"Good morning. Now, Ms. Barrow told me there are twins in this class.
Where are Katie and Joy Donovan?" Mr. Curtis looked at the girls. "Who is who?"
"I'm Katie," Katie spoke up.
"No, she's lying. That's Katie!" Luke said, laughing.
He pointed at Joy.
"Stop it, Luke!" Joy said angrily. "I'm Joy!"
"If you're Joy, then who is that?" Carlos said, pointing at Katie.
Everyone laughed, except for Mr. Curtis.
"Please settle down," said the teacher with a frown.
"Or I will have to ask Ms. Olson to come back."
After Mr. Curtis took attendance, the fourth graders had math.
"Joy," Mr. Curtis said, looking at Katie.
"What can you tell us about rounding six-digit numbers?"
Katie stared down at her math book.
"Joy," Mr. Curtis repeated sternly.
"You girls are making this very difficult."
Joy sighed. Ms. Barrow didn't have any trouble telling them apart.
Why was it so hard for Mr. Curtis?
"I know the answer." Larry raised his hand.
"Yes, Larry," Mr. Curtis said.
"It depends if you're rounding to the nearest hundred thousand, ten thousand, or thousand," Larry answered.
While Larry kept talking, Katie wrote a note to her sister.
It said: "A house divided against itself cannot stand . . ."–Abraham Lincoln.
Another note followed.
That means we have to stick together.
Do not answer unless Mr. Curtis calls you by the right name!
When Joy looked up, Katie was making a sign with her hand.
Joy recognized it right away—it was sign language for the word "twin."
Joy grinned and then signed the word back at her sister.
The Donovan twins were sticking together!
Laura, Luke, Olivia, Carlos, Katie, and Joy were walking home from school, all bundled up.
"What did Ms. Barrow say to you?" Laura asked.
"She said we didn't behave like leaders yesterday," Joy said sadly.
"She's right. We shouldn't have ignored Mr. Curtis when he called on us."
"Ms. Barrow talked to me too," Olivia said.
"She said protesting against my parents wasn't right.
Being rude to adults doesn't make you a leader."
"Well, Luke started it," said Katie.
"We were just standing by our principles."
"I guess it was kind of mean," Laura said to Joy.
Joy nodded. It had been funny to ignore Mr. Curtis yesterday.
But today she felt bad.
"Let's not talk about school.
It's Friday!" said Luke.
"Luke's right. Friday is a day for fun!
Who wants to ice skate on our pond?" Katie said.
"That sounds great," said Olivia.
"But we have chores to do, Katie.
And homework," said Joy.
She was thinking about the leaders project.
Katie rolled her eyes.
"It's Friday. Chores and homework are for Saturday and Sunday."
"We'll go home and get our skates," Carlos said.
"Me too," said Luke.
"Come on. It will be really fun," Katie said to her sister. "Please?"
Joy laughed. "Okay." Katie was right. Friday was a day for fun!
An hour later everyone was skating on the Donovans' pond.
"Whee! Watch this!" Laura said.
She skated on one leg and did a hop.
"That's not as cool as this."
Luke skated fast and then skidded to a stop.
"I've been practicing my spins."
Katie did a wobbly spin on one foot.
"Ouch!" she cried, landing on the ice.
Joy laughed as she watched her friends do tricks on the ice.
"Rats," said Katie. "It's getting dark."
"We'd better go home," said Carlos.
"You guys are so lucky to have a pond," Laura said.
Katie and Joy walked their friends to the driveway and waved good-bye.
Then they headed inside.
"Wait," said Joy.
"I'm going to collect eggs and check on the chickens."
She walked over to the chicken coop.
The chickens were sleeping side-by-side, huddled together for warmth.
"One, two, three, four, five," Joy counted.
"Five? One is missing!"
Frantic, Joy counted again.
There were only five.
Where was the sixth chicken?
She looked all around the chicken coop.
Had someone stolen it?
How could it have gotten out?
Joy walked into the kitchen, her head hanging.
"Mom, Katie," she said. "I have bad news."
"What's the matter, honey?" Mom asked.
She looked up from the stove, where she was stirring a pot of pasta.
"I lost a chicken," Joy said.
"How can you lose a chicken?" asked Katie.
Then she gasped.
"Wait—do you mean one is dead?"
"I don't know.
But this morning there were six.
Now there are only five," Joy said quietly.
"I'm a bad student, a bad leader, and a bad chicken keeper.
Grandpa will be disappointed in me."
"I'll help you look for it,"
Katie said, putting an arm around her sister.
She glanced out the dark window. "Tomorrow," she added.
"I will too," Mom said.
"And who knows?
Maybe the chicken will show up on its own."
She put her arm around Joy too.
The three Donovan girls stood by the window, staring out into the dark.
The wind was strong and it looked colder than ever.
"Why did I go ice skating instead of checking on the chickens?" Joy asked herself.
"Oh, little lost chicken, I hope you're warm and safe, wherever you are."
On Saturday morning Joy woke up at sunrise.
No one else was awake yet.
She quietly pulled on her clothes and tiptoed downstairs.
Last night she had made a to-do list.
Today she was determined to finish everything on it.
Her boots crunched on the icy grass as she walked into the yard.
"One, two, three, four, five."
Joy counted the chickens that were waddling around nearby.
One was still missing.
"Poor things," she said, noticing that their water feeder had frozen over.
She went to look for a stick to break up the ice.
Then Joy spotted something in the garden.
"Hey! What are you doing over there?"
It was the missing chicken!
Joy ran over and scooped up the chicken.
"Good thing you're alive," she said, patting its head.
"It's dangerous to escape, you know."
Joy put the chicken back in the coop.
But she still had a mystery to solve.
"How in the world did you get out?"
She circled the fence, looking for a hole, but didn't find anything.
Soon she heard Katie calling her for breakfast.
While she ate, Joy told Mom and Katie about how she'd found the chicken.
"Now I have to figure out how it escaped.
But first I'm going to work on my leader project.
Can I borrow your computer, Mom?"
"Of course," Mom said.
"Oh, and I'll need all your cotton balls and some shoe polish, Mom," Katie announced.
Mom stared at Katie.
"What on earth for?" she asked.
"I'm going to make an Abraham Lincoln beard," said Katie.
"To wear for my presentation on Monday."
Mom laughed. "I can't wait to see that!"
After breakfast the girls got to work.
Katie sat on the kitchen floor to make her beard.
Joy stayed at the table, reading about leaders on the Internet.
Magoo sat by Joy's feet, sniffing at Katie's shoe polish.
"Hey, Katie, what do you know about Harriet Tubman?" Joy asked.
Katie put down a cotton ball.
"Nothing. I've never heard of her! Who is she?"
"She was a slave, back when there were slaves in America.
And she was really smart.
So she escaped to freedom.
Then she helped other slaves escape too.
She risked her life helping them travel north, all the way to Pennsylvania and Canada!" explained Joy.
"She sounds brave," Katie said.
"She was," Joy said.
"She even worked for the Union army during the Civil War."
Katie smiled. "Hey! I wonder if she ever met Abraham Lincoln!"
She held up a few dyed cotton balls to her chin.
"Hello, Harriet," she said in her best Abraham Lincoln voice.
"Would you like to fight for the Union army?"
"I'm not a soldier, President Lincoln!
I'm a spy!" Joy cried.
The girls burst into giggles.
Just then the phone rang.
"I'll get it!" Katie jumped up.
"Hi, Olivia," she said. "No, I'm not doing anything."
Joy raised her eyebrows at Katie's mess on the floor.
Sometimes it was amazing how different she and her sister were.
"YES," Katie said loudly.
"Of course I want to practice ice skating turns!"
She hung up the phone and tapped Joy's shoulder.
"Put your books away.
Olivia's coming over.
We're going ice skating," she said.
"Magoo, stop it!"
Katie reached down and pulled a cotton ball from Magoo's mouth.
Joy glanced outside.
She wanted to practice ice skating turns with Olivia and Katie.
But it wasn't on her to-do list.
And she had finally gotten a great idea for her project.
Joy cleared her throat.
"I can't," she said.
"I've got a Harriet Tubman project to do!"
"Brr! It's cold out there!"
Olivia said as she walked into the kitchen.
"Who's ready to skate?"
"Guess who's not going with us," Katie said, frowning.
Olivia looked at the twins. "Joy? Why not?"
"I finally chose my leader.
So I need to work on my project.
Our presentations are only two days away!" said Joy.
Olivia nodded. "I understand," she said.
"You do?" asked Katie.
"Yes. Want us to help you?" Olivia asked Joy.
"Us?" Katie repeated.
Joy ignored her sister's comment and smiled at her friend.
"I can do the leader project by myself.
But I could use help solving the chicken mystery."
Harriet Tubman, she thought, would never ignore her pet chickens when they needed help.
"Count me in," said Olivia.
"Count me out," said Katie. "Those aren't my chickens."
"Would anyone like some hot cocoa?" Mom asked.
"Yes, please!" all three girls answered.
Olivia turned to Katie.
"Ms. Barrow told us we had to act like our leaders.
Would Abraham Lincoln go skating, while his friend—no, his sister—needed help?"
Katie sighed. "Probably not," she admitted.
"What do you need us to do, Joy?"
An hour later the girls were standing in front of the chicken coop.
Joy counted the chickens again.
"Oh no!" She gasped. "Now four are missing!"
Joy felt like crying.
But she knew a leader had to take charge.
"Someone needs to look for them," she said.
"Someone else needs to find how they are getting out.
And the third person needs to keep an eye on the two in here.
So they don't escape too!"
"I'll look for the chickens," Olivia offered.
"I'll check the coop for any holes," said Katie.
"Great, let's get to work!"
Joy broke the ice on the chickens' water feeder.
Then she refilled the chickens' food container.
A few minutes later, Olivia called, "Hey! Over here! I found something."
She was waving from underneath the tree house.
The twins ran over.
Olivia was standing near a pile of leaves and hay.
That was Grandpa's burn pile.
He hadn't burned anything since the day he got in trouble with the fire chief.
"It looks like some chickens have been using this as a nest."
Olivia pointed to six brown eggs lying on top of the pile.
They were almost the same color as the leaves.
"Wow," Joy said.
"That's why there were so few eggs lately."
"Why did they do that?" Katie asked.
Joy shrugged. "I don't know.
Maybe once they got out, they just looked for a soft place to lay their eggs."
"Now if we can just find the chickens . . . ," Olivia began.
"I know!" Katie cried. "Let's go in the tree house.
It's a great lookout spot!"
The girls scrambled up the tree house steps.
"Katie, you're a genius!
I see them!" Olivia cried.
She pointed to four chickens waddling around by the creek.
"Mission accomplished," Joy said after Olivia tossed the last chicken back into the coop.
"And I think I just discovered how they're getting out," Katie added.
She stuck her hand through a gap in the fence.
"The chicken wire here isn't attached to the post anymore."
"I'll ask Mom if I can use Dad's tools," Joy said.
"I can fix it before Grandpa gets back!"
"It will be just in time too," Olivia said, looking up.
Dark gray clouds were rolling over them.
"It looks like it's about to storm.
And it feels cold enough to snow!"
An icy wind blew as Joy stapled the chicken wire back to the fence post.
"Finished!" she said happily.
She locked the henhouse door and headed toward the house.
Something cold and wet landed on her face. Snow!
"Mom! Katie! It's snowing!" Joy cried, running into the kitchen.
"Finally," said Katie.
She and Olivia were at the table drinking another cup of cocoa.
"I love snow," Olivia said.
Joy put an arm around her friend.
"Thanks for coming over.
I'm really glad you helped me."
"That's what friends are for," Olivia said with a smile.
"I helped too, by the way," Katie said, poking her sister.
"Now hurry up and finish your project.
We need to play in the snow tomorrow!"
Joy laughed. "Don't worry. I'll get it done, I promise!"
Olivia was looking out the window, her eyes growing big.
"I should call my mom to pick me up.
It's snowing hard!"
After Olivia left, the twins sat in the living room.
Joy worked on her project while Katie flipped through a magazine.
Outside, everything was covered in white.
Soon Katie sighed. "I'm so bored."
Suddenly the phone rang.
"I'll get it!" Katie ran to the phone.
In the kitchen Mom looked at the clock.
"It's probably Dad and Grandpa," she said.
"They should be home soon."
"Hi, Dad!" Katie said into the phone.
"It's snowing really hard here too . . . Oh." Katie's voice dropped.
"Oh no. Okay . . ." She held out the phone to Mom.
"Dad needs to talk to you."
As Mom took the phone, Katie hurried back to Joy.
"Dad and Grandpa are stuck.
The highway is closed because of snow!" Katie said.
"Oh no. What will they do?" Joy asked.
"They'll go to a hotel in the next town,"
Mom said, joining the girls on the couch.
"Don't worry. The road will be plowed by morning," she added.
"This means we have another night by ourselves."
"Just us girls!" Joy said, smiling at her mom.
"We should watch a movie and eat popcorn!" Katie said.
"That sounds fun!" said Joy.
"That does sound fun," said Mom.
"But you girls have work to do, don't you?"
"Not me," Katie said. "I'm done with my project!"
Joy hesitated. "I still have work to do, but . . ."
"What do you think Harriet Tubman would do right now?" Mom asked.
Joy thought of a story she had read about Harriet Tubman.
When Harriet escaped to freedom, she walked all the way from Maryland to Pennsylvania.
That was about two hundred kilometers.
And Harriet never complained.
She never gave up.
She just kept going.
Joy sighed. "I'm going to keep working, Mom."
"Katie, how about we bake brownies in the kitchen instead?" Mom asked.
Katie nodded and followed her mom out of the living room.
"We need to leave Joy alone," Mom whispered.
"So she can finish her project."
"Okay," Katie whispered back.
She could try to be quiet.
"Let's see if we can find Grandpa's brownie recipe," Mom whispered.
An hour later Joy was still working in the living room.
Soon she smelled something burning.
"Ta-da!" Katie cried, marching in with a plate full of brownies.
"Katie, shh!" Mom reminded her.
"Oops." Katie grinned. "Ta-da," she whispered.
"Burnt brownies to help you concentrate!"
Joy giggled. She couldn't remember the last time Katie had baked something.
Or baked something for her.
"Thanks," she said. "That was really nice of you."
Katie gave Joy the sign for "twin" again, and Mom patted Joy on the shoulder.
"Good night, honey. Don't stay up too late."
"All right, Mom," Joy said.
She turned back to her report, determined to finish.
Joy woke up to the smell of pancakes.
"Mom is making pancakes?" she thought.
That was unusual.
Joy rushed downstairs.
"Grandpa!" she cried.
Grandpa was in front of the stove, flipping pancakes.
"Who wants pancakes?" he asked.
Joy gave her grandfather a huge hug.
"When did you get back?"
"Early this morning.
Your dad and I woke up at sunrise and drove straight here," he said.
"I heard you were up late, finishing schoolwork."
Joy grinned. "I was. But I finished my leaders project.
So I'm ready for pancakes and ready to play in the snow!"
Just then Katie bounced into the kitchen.
At the same time, Dad came in the backdoor, carrying firewood.
Mom followed him.
"Dad! Grandpa!" Katie cried, surprised.
"I can't wait to hear all about your weekend," Dad said.
He gave Katie's ponytail a playful tug.
"Isn't it nice that we're all home together again?" Mom said.
Grandpa set a huge stack of pancakes on the table.
"And isn't it nice that Grandpa is back to cook breakfast for us?" Katie replied. Mom laughed.
"So what did we miss while we were away?" Grandpa asked.
He winked at Mom.
"Besides cold cereal and burnt brownies?"
"Well, first of all, it was freezing outside," Katie began.
"And we thought we had an egg and chicken thief!" Joy added.
"But really some chickens were escaping through a hole in the fence!
And they were laying eggs in your burn pile, Grandpa," Katie said.
"Wow!" said Grandpa, surprised.
"I'm glad there wasn't a real thief!" said Dad.
"Then Joy fixed the hole in the fence all by herself," Katie said with her mouth full of pancakes.
"Wonderful!" said Grandpa.
"And tomorrow at school we're finally giving our reports on leaders," said Joy.
"Who did you end up choosing, Joy?" Grandpa asked.
"Harriet Tubman," Joy said.
"She spent her whole life working for something
important: getting slaves to
freedom." "Good choice," said
Dad. "Thanks." Joy poured maple syrup on her pancakes, thinking for a
minute. Would she ever be a great leader like Harriet
Tubman? "Dad," Joy said
slowly. "When you were a kid, what did you want to be when you grew
up?" Dad smiled. "I wanted to work in a park, taking care of
trees." "Now you take care of trees by helping people recycle!" Katie
said. Dad laughed. "I guess I
do." "What about you, Grandpa?" asked
Katie. Grandpa had been a mailman in Willow Creek for thirty
years. "I knew I wanted to be a mailman since I was nine years old," Grandpa
said. "I loved seeing people smile when they got a special letter or
package." "I always wanted to be a librarian," Mom chimed
in. "What about you
girls?" "I'm going to be the mayor of Willow Creek!" Katie
announced. Dad laughed. "That's perfect for
you." Joy grinned from ear to
ear. "I want to be a vet," she
said. "Those are great jobs," Grandpa
